solution:
At a fixed temperature a liquid and its vapour are in dynamic equilibrium, with the rate of evaporation equal to the rate of condensation.

a) Increasing the volume suddenly spreads the same amount of vapour through a larger space, so the vapour pressure FALLS immediately.

b) The rate of evaporation depends only on the temperature and the liquid surface, so it is UNCHANGED. The rate of condensation depends on how many vapour molecules strike the surface per second, which falls with the vapour concentration, so it DECREASES.

c) Since evaporation now exceeds condensation, more liquid vaporises until the vapour concentration builds back up and the two rates become equal again. Vapour pressure depends only on temperature, so the final vapour pressure is the SAME as the original value; only the amount of liquid has decreased.

By the law of chemical equilibrium, for \(2\text{SO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3(g)\),

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{SO}_3]^2}{[\text{SO}_2]^2[\text{O}_2]}\)

Substituting the equilibrium concentrations,

\(K_c = \dfrac{(1.90)^2}{(0.60)^2(0.82)} = \dfrac{3.61}{0.2952}\)

\(K_c = 12.23\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{L}\)

For a gas mixture the partial pressure of a component equals its volume fraction times the total pressure.

Given total pressure \(p = 10^5\,\text{Pa}\) and 40% by volume of \(\text{I}\) atoms,

\(p_{\text{I}} = 0.40 \times 10^5 = 4.0 \times 10^4\,\text{Pa}\)

\(p_{\text{I}_2} = 0.60 \times 10^5 = 6.0 \times 10^4\,\text{Pa}\)

For \(\text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{I}(g)\),

\(K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{I}}^2}{p_{\text{I}_2}} = \dfrac{(4.0 \times 10^4)^2}{6.0 \times 10^4} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^9}{6.0 \times 10^4}\)

\(K_p = 2.67 \times 10^4\,\text{Pa}\)

Pure solids and pure liquids have constant molar concentration and are omitted; so is water when it is the solvent of a dilute aqueous solution.

(i) \(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{NO}]^2[\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{NOCl}]^2}\)

(ii) \(\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2(s)\) and \(\text{CuO}(s)\) are solids, so \(K_c = [\text{NO}_2]^4[\text{O}_2]\)

(iii) The reaction occurs in dilute aqueous solution, so water is the solvent and is omitted: \(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}][\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5]}\). (If water is not treated as the solvent, \([\text{H}_2\text{O}]\) appears in the denominator as well.)

(iv) \(\text{Fe(OH)}_3(s)\) is a solid, so \(K_c = \dfrac{1}{[\text{Fe}^{3+}][\text{OH}^-]^3}\)

(v) \(\text{I}_2(s)\) is a solid, so \(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{IF}_5]^2}{[\text{F}_2]^5}\)

Using \(K_p = K_c(\text{R}T)^{\Delta n}\), so \(K_c = K_p/(\text{R}T)^{\Delta n}\), with \(\text{R} = 0.0831\,\text{bar L mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(\Delta n\) = (moles of gaseous products) - (moles of gaseous reactants).

(i) \(\Delta n = (2+1) - 2 = 1\), \(T = 500\,\text{K}\):

\(K_c = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-2}}{0.0831 \times 500} = \dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-2}}{41.55}\)

\(K_c = 4.33 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

(ii) Only \(\text{CO}_2\) is gaseous, so \(\Delta n = 1 - 0 = 1\), \(T = 1073\,\text{K}\):

\(K_c = \dfrac{167}{0.0831 \times 1073} = \dfrac{167}{89.17}\)

\(K_c = 1.87\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

The equilibrium constant of a reverse reaction is the reciprocal of that of the forward reaction, because reversing the equation interchanges the numerator and the denominator of the expression.

\(K_c(\text{reverse}) = \dfrac{1}{K_c(\text{forward})} = \dfrac{1}{6.3 \times 10^{14}}\)

\(K_c(\text{reverse}) = 1.6 \times 10^{-15}\)

The molar concentration of a pure solid or a pure liquid is its density divided by its molar mass. Both are fixed properties of the substance at a given temperature, so this concentration does not change however much of the solid or liquid is present — unlike a gas or a solute, whose concentration varies with the amount taken in a given volume.

Being constant, such a term can be absorbed into the equilibrium constant itself. Writing, for example, \(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{CaO}(s)][\text{CO}_2(g)]}{[\text{CaCO}_3(s)]}\) and multiplying through by the constant ratio \([\text{CaCO}_3(s)]/[\text{CaO}(s)]\) gives a new constant \(K'_c = [\text{CO}_2(g)]\).

Hence pure solids and pure liquids are simply left out of the equilibrium constant expression; only gases and species in solution appear in it. Note that they must still BE PRESENT for the heterogeneous equilibrium to exist.

Initial concentrations in the \(10\,\text{L}\) vessel:

\([\text{N}_2] = 0.482/10 = 0.0482\,\text{M}\), \([\text{O}_2] = 0.933/10 = 0.0933\,\text{M}\)

For \(2\text{N}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{N}_2\text{O}(g)\),

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{N}_2\text{O}]^2}{[\text{N}_2]^2[\text{O}_2]}\)

Since \(K_c = 2.0 \times 10^{-37}\) is extremely small, the extent of reaction is negligible and the reactant concentrations are effectively unchanged. Hence

\([\text{N}_2\text{O}]^2 = K_c[\text{N}_2]^2[\text{O}_2] = (2.0 \times 10^{-37})(0.0482)^2(0.0933) = 4.34 \times 10^{-41}\)

\([\text{N}_2\text{O}] = 6.6 \times 10^{-21}\,\text{M}\)

Equilibrium composition: \([\text{N}_2] = 0.0482\,\text{M}\), \([\text{O}_2] = 0.0933\,\text{M}\), \([\text{N}_2\text{O}] = 6.6 \times 10^{-21}\,\text{M}\).

From the stoichiometry of \(2\text{NO}(g) + \text{Br}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NOBr}(g)\), forming \(2\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{NOBr}\) consumes \(2\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{NO}\) and \(1\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{Br}_2\).

\(\text{NOBr}\) formed \(= 0.0518\,\text{mol}\)

\(\text{NO}\) consumed \(= 0.0518\,\text{mol}\)

\(\text{Br}_2\) consumed \(= 0.0518/2 = 0.0259\,\text{mol}\)

Therefore at equilibrium:

\(\text{NO} = 0.087 - 0.0518 = 0.0352\,\text{mol}\)

\(\text{Br}_2 = 0.0437 - 0.0259 = 0.0178\,\text{mol}\)

For \(2\text{SO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3(g)\), \(\Delta n = 2 - 3 = -1\).

Using \(K_p = K_c(\text{R}T)^{\Delta n}\),

\(K_c = K_p(\text{R}T)^{-\Delta n} = K_p(\text{R}T)\)

with \(\text{R} = 0.0831\,\text{bar L mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(T = 450\,\text{K}\):

\(K_c = (2.0 \times 10^{10})(0.0831 \times 450) = (2.0 \times 10^{10})(37.40)\)

\(K_c = 7.48 \times 10^{11}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\text{L}\)

\(2\text{HI}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g)\)

Initial pressure of \(\text{HI} = 0.2\,\text{atm}\); at equilibrium \(p_{\text{HI}} = 0.04\,\text{atm}\).

\(\text{HI}\) decomposed \(= 0.2 - 0.04 = 0.16\,\text{atm}\)

From the stoichiometry, \(2\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{HI}\) give \(1\,\text{mol}\) each of \(\text{H}_2\) and \(\text{I}_2\), so

\(p_{\text{H}_2} = p_{\text{I}_2} = 0.16/2 = 0.08\,\text{atm}\)

\(K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{H}_2}\,p_{\text{I}_2}}{p_{\text{HI}}^2} = \dfrac{(0.08)(0.08)}{(0.04)^2} = \dfrac{0.0064}{0.0016}\)

\(K_p = 4.0\) (dimensionless, since \(\Delta n = 0\))

Concentrations in the \(20\,\text{L}\) vessel:

\([\text{N}_2] = 1.57/20 = 0.0785\,\text{M}\), \([\text{H}_2] = 1.92/20 = 0.096\,\text{M}\), \([\text{NH}_3] = 8.13/20 = 0.4065\,\text{M}\)

The reaction quotient is defined like \(K_c\) but with the concentrations actually present:

\(Q_c = \dfrac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3} = \dfrac{(0.4065)^2}{(0.0785)(0.096)^3} = \dfrac{0.1652}{6.95 \times 10^{-5}}\)

\(Q_c = 2.38 \times 10^3\)

Since \(Q_c\ (2.38 \times 10^3) \neq K_c\ (1.7 \times 10^2)\), the mixture is NOT at equilibrium.

As \(Q_c > K_c\), the reaction proceeds in the REVERSE direction — \(\text{NH}_3\) decomposes to \(\text{N}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\) until \(Q_c\) falls to \(K_c\).

In a \(K_c\) expression the species in the NUMERATOR are the products and those in the DENOMINATOR are the reactants, and each exponent is that species' stoichiometric coefficient.

Numerator: \([\text{NH}_3]^4[\text{O}_2]^5\) means \(4\,\text{NH}_3\) and \(5\,\text{O}_2\) are products.

Denominator: \([\text{NO}]^4[\text{H}_2\text{O}]^6\) means \(4\,\text{NO}\) and \(6\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\) are reactants.

The balanced chemical equation is

\(4\text{NO}(g) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons 4\text{NH}_3(g) + 5\text{O}_2(g)\)

(Check: N 4 = 4; O 4 + 6 = 10 = 5 x 2; H 12 = 12.)

\(\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)

40% of the \(1\,\text{mol}\) of water reacts, i.e. \(0.4\,\text{mol}\), consuming \(0.4\,\text{mol}\) of \(\text{CO}\) and forming \(0.4\,\text{mol}\) each of \(\text{H}_2\) and \(\text{CO}_2\).

At equilibrium (in \(10\,\text{L}\)):

\(\text{H}_2\text{O} = \text{CO} = 0.6\,\text{mol}\); \(\text{H}_2 = \text{CO}_2 = 0.4\,\text{mol}\)

Since \(\Delta n = 0\), the volume cancels and mole numbers may be used directly:

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{H}_2][\text{CO}_2]}{[\text{H}_2\text{O}][\text{CO}]} = \dfrac{(0.4)(0.4)}{(0.6)(0.6)} = \dfrac{0.16}{0.36}\)

\(K_c = 0.44\)

\(\text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}(g)\), \(K_c = 54.8\)

Starting from \(\text{HI}\) alone, its decomposition produces \(\text{H}_2\) and \(\text{I}_2\) in equal amounts, so let

\([\text{H}_2] = [\text{I}_2] = x\), with \([\text{HI}] = 0.5\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) at equilibrium.

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]} = \dfrac{(0.5)^2}{x^2} = 54.8\)

\(x^2 = \dfrac{0.25}{54.8} = 4.562 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(x = 6.75 \times 10^{-2}\)

\([\text{H}_2] = [\text{I}_2] = 0.068\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

\(2\text{ICl}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{I}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\), \(K_c = 0.14\)

Let \(x\) be the equilibrium concentration of \(\text{I}_2\) (and of \(\text{Cl}_2\)); then \(2x\) of \(\text{ICl}\) has reacted.

At equilibrium: \([\text{ICl}] = 0.78 - 2x\), \([\text{I}_2] = [\text{Cl}_2] = x\)

\(K_c = \dfrac{x^2}{(0.78-2x)^2} = 0.14\)

Taking the square root of both sides (both quantities are positive),

\(\dfrac{x}{0.78-2x} = \sqrt{0.14} = 0.3742\)

\(x = 0.2919 - 0.7483x\), so \(1.7483x = 0.2919\) and \(x = 0.167\)

\([\text{I}_2] = [\text{Cl}_2] = 0.167\,\text{M}\)

\([\text{ICl}] = 0.78 - 2(0.167) = 0.446\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_2\text{H}_4(g) + \text{H}_2(g)\), \(K_p = 0.04\,\text{atm}\)

Let \(x\,\text{atm}\) be the fall in the pressure of \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\).

Initial: \(p_{\text{C}_2\text{H}_6} = 4.0\,\text{atm}\), others zero.

At equilibrium: \(p_{\text{C}_2\text{H}_6} = (4.0-x)\), \(p_{\text{C}_2\text{H}_4} = p_{\text{H}_2} = x\)

\(K_p = \dfrac{x \cdot x}{4.0-x} = 0.04\)

\(x^2 + 0.04x - 0.16 = 0\)

\(x = \dfrac{-0.04 + \sqrt{(0.04)^2 + 4(0.16)}}{2} = \dfrac{-0.04 + 0.8010}{2} = 0.3805\)

(The negative root is rejected as a pressure cannot be negative.)

\(p_{\text{C}_2\text{H}_6} = 4.0 - 0.3805 = 3.62\,\text{atm}\)

(i) Water is neither in excess nor the solvent here, so it appears in the expression:

\(Q_c = \dfrac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}][\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}]}\)

(ii) \(0.171\,\text{mol}\) of ester formed consumes \(0.171\,\text{mol}\) each of acid and ethanol and forms \(0.171\,\text{mol}\) of water.

At equilibrium: acid \(= 1.00-0.171 = 0.829\); ethanol \(= 0.18-0.171 = 0.009\); ester \(=\) water \(= 0.171\,\text{mol}\).

Since \(\Delta n = 0\) the volume cancels:

\(K_c = \dfrac{(0.171)(0.171)}{(0.829)(0.009)} = \dfrac{0.02924}{0.007461}\)

\(K_c = 3.92\)

(iii) At the stated instant: acid \(= 1.0-0.214 = 0.786\); ethanol \(= 0.5-0.214 = 0.286\); ester \(=\) water \(= 0.214\,\text{mol}\).

\(Q_c = \dfrac{(0.214)(0.214)}{(0.786)(0.286)} = \dfrac{0.04580}{0.2248} = 0.204\)

Since \(Q_c\ (0.204) < K_c\ (3.92)\), equilibrium has NOT been reached; the reaction is still proceeding in the forward direction.

\(\text{PCl}_5(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\)

Starting from pure \(\text{PCl}_5\), the two products are formed in equal amounts, so let

\([\text{PCl}_3] = [\text{Cl}_2] = x\), with \([\text{PCl}_5] = 0.5 \times 10^{-1} = 0.05\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\).

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{PCl}_3][\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{PCl}_5]} = \dfrac{x^2}{0.05} = 8.3 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(x^2 = 4.15 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(x = 2.04 \times 10^{-2}\)

\([\text{PCl}_3] = [\text{Cl}_2] = 2.04 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

\(\text{FeO}(s) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\); the solids are omitted, so

\(K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{CO}_2}}{p_{\text{CO}}} = 0.265\)

First test the direction with the reaction quotient:

\(Q_p = 0.80/1.4 = 0.571 > K_p\), so the reaction proceeds in the REVERSE direction and \(\text{CO}_2\) is consumed.

Let \(y\,\text{atm}\) be the fall in \(p_{\text{CO}_2}\); then \(p_{\text{CO}}\) rises by the same amount (1 : 1 stoichiometry).

\(\dfrac{0.80-y}{1.4+y} = 0.265\)

\(0.80 - y = 0.371 + 0.265y\), so \(1.265y = 0.429\) and \(y = 0.339\)

\(p_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.80 - 0.339 = 0.461\,\text{atm}\)

\(p_{\text{CO}} = 1.4 + 0.339 = 1.739\,\text{atm}\)

\(Q_c = \dfrac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3} = \dfrac{(0.5)^2}{(3.0)(2.0)^3} = \dfrac{0.25}{24}\)

\(Q_c = 1.04 \times 10^{-2}\)

Since \(Q_c\ (0.0104) \neq K_c\ (0.061)\), the reaction is NOT at equilibrium.

As \(Q_c < K_c\), the reaction proceeds in the FORWARD direction — more \(\text{NH}_3\) is formed from \(\text{N}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\) until \(Q_c\) rises to \(K_c\).

\(2\text{BrCl}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Br}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\), \(K_c = 32\)

Let \(x\) be the equilibrium concentration of \(\text{Br}_2\) (and of \(\text{Cl}_2\)); then \(2x\) of \(\text{BrCl}\) has reacted.

At equilibrium: \([\text{BrCl}] = 3.3 \times 10^{-3} - 2x\), \([\text{Br}_2] = [\text{Cl}_2] = x\)

\(K_c = \dfrac{x^2}{(3.3 \times 10^{-3} - 2x)^2} = 32\)

Taking square roots, \(\dfrac{x}{3.3 \times 10^{-3} - 2x} = \sqrt{32} = 5.657\)

\(x = 1.867 \times 10^{-2} - 11.314x\), so \(12.314x = 1.867 \times 10^{-2}\) and \(x = 1.516 \times 10^{-3}\)

\([\text{BrCl}] = 3.3 \times 10^{-3} - 2(1.516 \times 10^{-3})\)

\([\text{BrCl}] = 2.7 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

Take \(100\,\text{g}\) of the gas mixture: \(90.55\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CO}\) and \(9.45\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{CO}_2\).

Molar masses: \(\text{CO} = 28\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\), \(\text{CO}_2 = 44\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\).

\(n_{\text{CO}} = 90.55/28 = 3.234\,\text{mol}\); \(n_{\text{CO}_2} = 9.45/44 = 0.2148\,\text{mol}\); total \(= 3.449\,\text{mol}\)

By Dalton's law the partial pressure is the mole fraction times the total pressure \((1\,\text{atm})\):

\(p_{\text{CO}} = 3.234/3.449 = 0.9377\,\text{atm}\); \(p_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.0623\,\text{atm}\)

Carbon is a solid and is omitted:

\(K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{CO}}^2}{p_{\text{CO}_2}} = \dfrac{(0.9377)^2}{0.0623} = 14.12\,\text{atm}\)

With \(\Delta n = 2-1 = 1\), \(\text{R} = 0.0821\,\text{L atm mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\) and \(T = 1127\,\text{K}\):

\(K_c = \dfrac{K_p}{(\text{R}T)^{\Delta n}} = \dfrac{14.12}{0.0821 \times 1127} = \dfrac{14.12}{92.53}\)

\(K_c = 0.153\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)

a) The standard Gibbs energy change is the sum for the products minus that for the reactants, each weighted by its coefficient; \(\Delta_f G^\ominus\) of an element in its standard state is zero.

\(\Delta G^\ominus = \Delta_f G^\ominus(\text{NO}_2) - \left[\Delta_f G^\ominus(\text{NO}) + \tfrac{1}{2}\Delta_f G^\ominus(\text{O}_2)\right]\)

\(\Delta G^\ominus = 52.0 - [87.0 + 0] = -35.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)

b) Using \(\Delta G^\ominus = -\text{R}T\ln K\), i.e. \(K = e^{-\Delta G^\ominus/\text{R}T}\), with \(\text{R} = 8.314\,\text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(T = 298\,\text{K}\):

\(\ln K = \dfrac{35.0 \times 10^3}{8.314 \times 298} = \dfrac{35000}{2477.6} = 14.13\)

\(K = e^{14.13}\)

\(K = 1.36 \times 10^6\)

(The large positive \(K\) is consistent with the negative \(\Delta G^\ominus\): the products predominate.)

By Le Chatelier's principle, decreasing the pressure by increasing the volume shifts an equilibrium toward the side with MORE moles of gas. Only gaseous species count.

(a) \(\text{PCl}_5(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\): \(1 \rightarrow 2\) moles of gas, \(\Delta n = +1\). The equilibrium shifts forward, so the number of moles of products INCREASES.

(b) \(\text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaCO}_3(s)\): \(1 \rightarrow 0\) moles of gas, \(\Delta n = -1\). The equilibrium shifts backward (toward \(\text{CO}_2\)), so the moles of the product \(\text{CaCO}_3\) DECREASE.

(c) \(3\text{Fe}(s) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4(s) + 4\text{H}_2(g)\): \(4 \rightarrow 4\) moles of gas, \(\Delta n = 0\). There is no shift, so the number of moles of products REMAINS THE SAME.

An equilibrium is affected by a pressure change only if \(\Delta n_{\text{gas}} \neq 0\); increasing the pressure shifts it toward the side with FEWER moles of gas.

(i) \(\text{COCl}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{CO} + \text{Cl}_2\): \(1 \rightarrow 2\), affected; shifts BACKWARD.

(ii) \(\text{CH}_4 + 2\text{S}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{CS}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{S}\): \(3 \rightarrow 3\), \(\Delta n = 0\); NOT affected.

(iii) \(\text{CO}_2 + \text{C}(s) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}\): gaseous \(1 \rightarrow 2\), affected; shifts BACKWARD.

(iv) \(2\text{H}_2 + \text{CO} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH}\): \(3 \rightarrow 1\), affected; shifts FORWARD.

(v) \(\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2\): gaseous \(0 \rightarrow 1\), affected; shifts BACKWARD.

(vi) \(4\text{NH}_3 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 4\text{NO} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\): \(9 \rightarrow 10\), affected; shifts BACKWARD.

So all except (ii) are affected.

Only \(\text{HBr}\) is present initially, so the reaction runs in reverse. For

\(2\text{HBr}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g) + \text{Br}_2(g)\), \(K' = \dfrac{1}{K} = \dfrac{1}{1.6 \times 10^5} = 6.25 \times 10^{-6}\)

Let \(p_{\text{H}_2} = p_{\text{Br}_2} = x\,\text{bar}\); then \(p_{\text{HBr}} = (10.0 - 2x)\,\text{bar}\).

\(K' = \dfrac{x^2}{(10.0-2x)^2} = 6.25 \times 10^{-6}\)

Taking square roots, \(\dfrac{x}{10.0-2x} = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}\)

\(x = 0.025 - 5.0 \times 10^{-3}x\), so \(1.005x = 0.025\) and \(x = 0.0249\)

\(p_{\text{H}_2} = p_{\text{Br}_2} = 2.49 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{bar}\)

\(p_{\text{HBr}} = 10.0 - 2(0.0249) = 9.95\,\text{bar}\)

(a) \(K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{CO}} \cdot p_{\text{H}_2}^3}{p_{\text{CH}_4} \cdot p_{\text{H}_2\text{O}}}\)

(b) The value of \(K_p\) depends ONLY on temperature.

(i) Increasing the pressure: \(K_p\) is UNCHANGED. Since \(\Delta n = 4 - 2 = +2\), the equilibrium shifts backward, so the mixture becomes richer in \(\text{CH}_4\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) and poorer in \(\text{CO}\) and \(\text{H}_2\).

(ii) Increasing the temperature: the reaction is endothermic, so heat behaves as a reactant and the equilibrium shifts forward. \(K_p\) INCREASES and the yield of \(\text{CO}\) and \(\text{H}_2\) rises.

(iii) Using a catalyst: \(K_p\) is UNCHANGED and the equilibrium composition is UNCHANGED. A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is merely reached sooner.

For \(2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)\), Le Chatelier's principle says the system shifts so as to partly undo the change imposed.

a) Addition of \(\text{H}_2\) — a reactant is added, so the equilibrium shifts FORWARD and more \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\) is formed.

b) Addition of \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\) — the product is added, so the equilibrium shifts BACKWARD and \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\) decomposes to \(\text{H}_2\) and \(\text{CO}\).

c) Removal of \(\text{CO}\) — a reactant is removed, so the equilibrium shifts BACKWARD to replace it, and \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\) decreases.

d) Removal of \(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}\) — the product is removed, so the equilibrium shifts FORWARD to replace it, consuming more \(\text{H}_2\) and \(\text{CO}\).

a) \(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{PCl}_3][\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{PCl}_5]}\)

b) The equilibrium constant of the reverse reaction is the reciprocal of the forward one:

\(K_c(\text{reverse}) = \dfrac{1}{8.3 \times 10^{-3}} = 1.2 \times 10^2\)

c) \(K_c\) is a function of temperature ALONE.

(i) Adding more \(\text{PCl}_5\): NO change in \(K_c\). (The equilibrium shifts forward until the ratio of concentrations returns to the same \(K_c\).)

(ii) Increasing the pressure: NO change in \(K_c\). (The position of equilibrium shifts backward because \(\Delta n = +1\), but the constant itself is unaltered.)

(iii) Increasing the temperature: \(K_c\) INCREASES, because \(\Delta_r H^\ominus = +124.0\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) shows the forward reaction is endothermic and is therefore favoured by heating.

[Textbook answer-key error, and it is self-refuting on the stem's own \(K_p\). The key prints \(p_{\text{H}_2} = 0.96\,\text{bar}\). That value is not the hydrogen pressure — it is what is LEFT of each reactant: solving \(x/(4.0-x) = \sqrt{10.1} = 3.178\) gives \(x = 3.0426\), and \(4.0 - 3.0426 = 0.9574 \approx 0.96\). Taking the key at face value inverts the equilibrium: with \(p_{\text{H}_2} = p_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.9574\) and \(p_{\text{CO}} = p_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = 3.0426\), the constant comes out \(0.0990 = 1/10.1\) — the RECIPROCAL of the \(K_p\) the question supplies. The answer below substitutes back to \(10.100\).] \(\text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2(g)\), \(K_p = 10.1\)

Let \(x\,\text{bar}\) be the fall in the pressure of each reactant; the stoichiometry is 1 : 1 : 1 : 1.

Initial: \(p_{\text{CO}} = p_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = 4.0\,\text{bar}\), products zero.

At equilibrium: \(p_{\text{CO}} = p_{\text{H}_2\text{O}} = (4.0-x)\), \(p_{\text{CO}_2} = p_{\text{H}_2} = x\)

\(K_p = \dfrac{x \cdot x}{(4.0-x)(4.0-x)} = 10.1\)

Taking square roots, \(\dfrac{x}{4.0-x} = \sqrt{10.1} = 3.178\)

\(x = 12.71 - 3.178x\), so \(4.178x = 12.71\) and \(x = 3.04\)

\(p_{\text{H}_2} = 3.04\,\text{bar}\)

(Since \(\Delta n = 0\), \(K_p\) is dimensionless and no unit conversion is needed.)

The magnitude of \(K_c\) tells how far a reaction goes: \(K_c > 10^3\) means products predominate, \(K_c < 10^{-3}\) means reactants predominate, and only when \(K_c\) lies between \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^3\) are appreciable amounts of BOTH present.

a) \(K_c = 5 \times 10^{-39}\), far below \(10^{-3}\): almost entirely reactants \((\text{Cl}_2)\).

b) \(K_c = 3.7 \times 10^{8}\), far above \(10^{3}\): almost entirely product \((\text{NOCl})\).

c) \(K_c = 1.8\), which lies in the range \(10^{-3}\) to \(10^{3}\): APPRECIABLE concentrations of both reactants and products.

Only reaction (c) has appreciable concentrations of reactants and products.

For \(3\text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{O}_3(g)\),

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{O}_3]^2}{[\text{O}_2]^3}\)

Rearranging and substituting \(K_c = 2.0 \times 10^{-50}\) and \([\text{O}_2] = 1.6 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\):

\([\text{O}_3]^2 = K_c[\text{O}_2]^3 = (2.0 \times 10^{-50})(1.6 \times 10^{-2})^3\)

\([\text{O}_3]^2 = (2.0 \times 10^{-50})(4.096 \times 10^{-6}) = 8.19 \times 10^{-56}\)

\([\text{O}_3] = 2.86 \times 10^{-28}\,\text{M}\)

The extremely small value reflects the very small \(K_c\): ozone is present only in traces at equilibrium.

The flask has a volume of \(1\,\text{L}\), so mole numbers are numerically equal to molar concentrations.

\([\text{CO}] = 0.30\,\text{M}\), \([\text{H}_2] = 0.10\,\text{M}\), \([\text{H}_2\text{O}] = 0.02\,\text{M}\)

For \(\text{CO}(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_4(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g)\),

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{CH}_4][\text{H}_2\text{O}]}{[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2]^3}\)

Rearranging for the unknown,

\([\text{CH}_4] = \dfrac{K_c[\text{CO}][\text{H}_2]^3}{[\text{H}_2\text{O}]} = \dfrac{(3.90)(0.30)(0.10)^3}{0.02} = \dfrac{1.17 \times 10^{-3}}{0.02}\)

\([\text{CH}_4] = 5.85 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
